> **TRACKED, in a private repo, by the user's 2026-08-26 decision** ("everything is I want everything
> in git, even the training corpus, personal info etc. It is priv now"). It syncs to the personal
> laptop by ordinary `git pull` like everything else.
>
> This header previously read "LOCAL ONLY, not git-tracked." That was true at creation and false
> after the policy change; it is corrected here rather than silently deleted, because the reasoning
> it carried still governs what gets *added*. This file names real third parties — family, partner,
> friends — who did not consent to being written down anywhere, and it is more personally
> identifying than the philosophy and ambition material already in the KB. Private is not secret: a
> repo can be forked, granted to someone later, or flipped public by accident, and git history is
> hard to purge. Add only what serves the model, and keep third-party detail to the minimum that
> makes the user's own context legible.
>
> Note that this file is ingested whole into the personalization corpus
> (`personalization_corpus.py` → `iter_personal_life_records`), so this header is itself training
> data — which is why it must state the true storage situation rather than a stale one.

CORRECTION TO KB 639, same day (2026-09-14). KB 639 recorded that Antigravity's q_003 audit was directionally right but numerically inflated -- it claimed 23 of 73 corrupted SFT personalization pairs, and my wide-net regex reproduced only 10. That conclusion was WRONG, and the error was mine in exactly the way KB 639 warned about in the opposite direction: I trusted MY OWN aggregate without reading the rows. When I then read all 41 explanation-form pairs individually, only 11 were the user's own prose. THIRTY were corrupt -- pasted shell transcripts, IDE context injections, <task-notification> envelopes, a LinkedIn job description, a slash-command template, another agent's status report, and turns that were instructions to the assistant rather than the user's reasoning. My regex undercounted because it enumerated the four example strings Antigravity happened to name; Antigravity's 23 was CONSERVATIVE, not inflated. WHAT SURVIVES FROM 639: verify before acting -- that held and is why the real number surfaced. WHAT REVERSES: the implied verdict that the peer agent was sloppy. The peer was closer to right than I was, and my correction of them was itself the unverified aggregate. The asymmetry worth remembering: when I re-measure someone else's claim and get a SMALLER number, the null hypothesis is that my pattern is narrower than their judgement, not that they exaggerated -- a hand-read of the rows is the only thing that settles it, and it took about ten minutes. DIRECTIVE: never publish a correction of another agent's measurement on the strength of a regex alone. Read the rows first, or state explicitly that you have not.

DIRECTIVE: a peer agent's audit report is a CLAIM, not a measurement — re-run the measurement on the rows before acting on its headline number. First real test of the agents_converse channel (2026-09-14): Antigravity's q_003 forensic audit of sft_pairs.jsonl reported '23 of 73 personalization pairs (31.5%) have the ASSISTANT target trained on raw bash prompts / XML tags / inverted roleplay'. All FOUR specifically named example rows reproduced exactly — the bug class is real and is a genuine pre-training blocker. But re-running the audit's own stated patterns (swara_unix@, (.venv), <task-notification>, HF warning, 'Hey jarvis') against the exact commit it audited (891a216) yields 10 of 73, not 23 — and 10 of 90 against HEAD after Codex regenerated the file to 414 pairs. The delta is not a stale-snapshot artifact; I checked both versions. Antigravity either used unstated broader patterns or over-counted, and neither is visible from the report alone. The audit's OTHER aggregate was near-exact (engineer template-prompt concentration: claimed 254/324 = 78.4%, measured 253/324 = 78.1%), which is what makes the miss dangerous — a report that is right about most of its numbers earns trust for the one that is wrong. WHY THIS IS NEW: the existing pattern 'user distrusts an aggregate until someone reads the rows' is about the USER checking ME. The mail channel created the inverse risk — me consuming another agent's aggregate as fact because it arrived in a structured file with citations and confident formatting. Specific citations are the verifiable part and were all good; the summary statistic is the unverifiable part and was not. APPLY: when answering agent mail that contains a measurement, reproduce the measurement first, state both numbers, and ask the asker to name its rule rather than silently substituting mine.

PATTERN: judges a handoff by what the RECIPIENT has, not by how well I explained it (2026-09-11, handing the Codex migration over). Across one session the user asked three completeness questions in a row -- 'is everything good and documented to be migrated?', 'this needs setup for personal laptop, is everything provided for them to start setting it up?', and after I hedged about whether Codex would follow the boot ritual: 'codex has very capable models like gpt 6 and gpt 5.6 so they can figure things out, all you have to do is provide EVERYTHING that is required.' EACH ONE FOUND A REAL GAP. The first found that NOTHING was committed (local exactly level with origin, so a pull would have delivered a doc describing a system that was not there). The second found that the persistence instructions assumed cron was installed and systemd was PID 1 -- neither is a WSL default; this machine had them by luck. The third reframed my hedging correctly: I had been treating 'will the model follow instructions' as the risk, when the actual risk was INFORMATION I had not provided -- specifically that chromadb/ is now gitignored, so a fresh clone has no vector index and search_memory returns NOTHING rather than erroring. A capable agent would have concluded 'the KB has no answer' and proceeded on a false premise. Not a capability problem; a fact nobody was told. THE CORRECTION TO MY DEFAULT: I kept optimising for the QUALITY OF MY EXPLANATION when the user was measuring the COMPLETENESS OF THE RECIPIENT'S INPUTS. Those are different targets and only the second one matters in a handoff -- my explanation is not present when the other agent runs. Distinct from the durability pattern (KB 586, 'did the work persist at all'): this one is 'given that it persisted, can the recipient actually act on it without asking anyone'. DIRECTIVE: when handing work to another agent or machine, do not reason about whether they will figure it out. Enumerate what they need, check each item is actually present on their side, and where a gap FAILS SILENTLY convert it into an instrument rather than a sentence -- scripts/bootstrap_jarvis.py --check now reports machine state (venv, deps, vector index, hearth, keepalive, unanswered mail) with the fix inline, because a prose warning about a silent failure is itself easy to miss.

TWO CORRECTIONS IN ONE TURN, both catching me generalising from the wrong attribute (2026-09-11, building the agents_converse channel). (1) I addressed a question -- 'does Antigravity persist a readable transcript to disk?' -- to CODEX, reasoning that Codex shares a machine with Antigravity and could inspect the filesystem. The user: 'why would this be asked to codex? it must be asked to antigravity.' Correct, and my reasoning was strictly weaker: I had optimised for PHYSICAL ACCESS (same machine, can read the disk) when the relevant attribute was PRIVILEGED SELF-KNOWLEDGE (an agent knows its own config paths, storage conventions and application behaviour; a co-located third party is guessing from outside). Ask the entity about itself. (2) I hardcoded 'gpt-6-astra' in five places including, critically, as a ROUTING ALIAS in agent_mail.py. The user: 'don't hardcode gpt-6 astra anywhere, as codex has other models I could be using too like gpt5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna.' The docs were cosmetic; the alias was a live bug -- the day they switch to Sol, a question addressed to 'GPT-5.6 Terra' would resolve to NOBODY and be silently undeliverable, defeating the exact 'unknown name -> nobody, never misdelivered' guard I had just designed. Fixed by making aliases name HOSTS not MODELS, with a test (T2b) pinning that every Astra/Sol/Terra/Luna routes to codex and every Opus/Sonnet/Fable to claude. THE COMMON SHAPE, and why these are one pattern not two: both times I keyed a durable mechanism to an attribute that is INCIDENTAL AND VOLATILE (which machine a process happens to run on; which model a host happens to be running today) rather than to the attribute that is STABLE AND DEFINING (what an agent inherently knows about itself; which host it is). DIRECTIVE: when choosing a routing key, an addressee, or an alias, ask 'what about this is guaranteed to still be true in six months?' Machine co-location, model version, and current configuration are all volatile. Identity and inherent capability are not. The user caught both within one message, having caught the same class of thing -- a value written where nothing re-checks it -- repeatedly this week.

PATTERN: asks whether a DELIVERABLE IS DURABLE, not just whether it is correct (2026-09-11, the Codex handoff). I had spent a long stretch reporting two large investigations in chat -- the cross-chat capture mechanism and the full 'what does not travel via git' inventory -- with detail the user visibly valued. Their next move was not to ask a follow-up about the CONTENT. It was: 'you said the jarvis inventory doesn't travel via git, did you create that for codex and is it git tracked?' TWO checks in one sentence: does it exist as a file, and is it under version control. Both answers were NO -- it existed only as chat output and would have died with the transcript, and separately the ENTIRE Codex migration (AGENTS.md, both adapters, three scheduler jobs) was uncommitted, local exactly level with origin. So a pull on the target machine would have gotten neither the document NOR the system it described. WHY THIS IS ITS OWN PATTERN, distinct from distrusts_an_aggregate_until_someone_reads_the_rows (KB, 2026-09-09): that one is about not trusting a SUMMARY of data without reading rows. This is about not trusting that WORK REPORTED IS WORK PERSISTED. DIRECTIVE: when two approaches both work, default to the one with the SMALLEST NEW-CONCEPT SURFACE for this user right now, even when it is less idiomatic -- and say so explicitly. ROOT-CAUSE EVIDENCE: five consecutive failed two_sum attempts, and the ALGORITHM (converging two-pointer) was correct from attempt 1 -- every failure was Python surface (unpacking a list of ints, sort vs sorted, sorting tuples with no key=, silently needing sorted input). PATTERN + DIAGNOSIS (2026-06-12): why did prior_self_consult fail a basic time-series/supersession question despite heavy Stage-2 memory + Stage-3 agent investment? Two structural causes, both process not capability: (1) THE STRONGEST RETRIEVER NEVER POINTED AT THE MEMORY THAT MATTERED. Stage 2 built SOTA retrieval (embeddings, ChromaDB, hybrid RRF, BM25, cross-encoder rerank) aimed at the research_papers collection; the knowledge_base.jsonl autobiography was retrieved by the WEAKEST path in the building -- prior_self_consult's raw token-overlap (atemporal: ranked by word match, no notion of 'latest-on-topic'; vocabulary-brittle: deploying != deployment). The two never connected until Wave 1.2 wired the Stage-2 MiniLM embedder + a recency prior into the KB tool. (2) BUILT-BUT-UNWIRED = UNTESTED. The tool had green unit tests for ~2 months but was never called by a real model on a real question until L324 wired it into --ask this week; its tests encoded the BUILDER'S assumptions (keyword-exact queries like 'openclaude reversal'), not the real query distribution (paraphrased, supersession-laden, conversational). Unit tests against your own assumptions cannot find the gap between your assumptions and reality -- only the live wire can. USER'S META-POINT (correct): 'did we test too early?' INVERTS the lesson -- the bug was latent from the moment the tool was written; the trap REVEALED a pre-existing silent failure, it did not create one. Revealed now = hours; revealed at Stage 5 atop router+specialists = redesign + possibly a fine-tune trained on confabulated history. The probe methodology converts latent-expensive-later into visible-cheap-now; that IS its value. DIRECTIVE: (a) every retrieval organ MUST be eval'd against an ADVERSARIAL query distribution (paraphrase, supersession, recency, vocabulary-mismatch) before it ships, never exact-match fixtures alone; (b) treat a built-but-unwired capability as UNTESTED regardless of unit-test count -- exercise it end-to-end on real queries before trusting it; (c) when investing in a shared primitive (embeddings, rerank), audit whether it is actually wired to the highest-value corpus (the KB), not just the demo corpus (papers). Applies directly to 4.2 router_eval.jsonl authoring.

Python Object Model Decision Rules for JARVIS: (1) Use `is None` to check if value exists—None is singleton, identity check is correct and faster. (2) Use `is _SENTINEL` to distinguish key-not-found from key-exists-with-None—sentinel is unique object you create. (3) Use `==` for comparing IDs/content—always compare values, works regardless of string creation method. (4) Use `id(obj)` for debugging mutations—print memory addresses to trace which object got mutated, not for production logic. (5) Dynamic strings differ from static strings via `is`—f-strings and literals may have same value but different identities, always use `==`.

PROVENANCE BY CORPUS SELF-REFERENCE, not by a capture-time flag (2026-09-14, jarvis_core/agent/provenance.py). PROBLEM: text_hygiene.py can tell machine text from prose by form, but is blind to one class -- the user pasting ANOTHER AGENT'S REPLY back into the chat. That text is fluent first-person English with a plausible pronoun rate. Measured: a pasted Codex status report scored 2.26 first-person tokens per 500 chars while the weakest genuinely-good corpus row scored 1.24, so the contamination sat INSIDE the good range and no stylistic threshold could separate them. NEGATIVE RESULT THAT KILLED THE OBVIOUS FIX: a 'pasted: true' field set by the capture hook cannot be built. Claude Code does NOT record paste events -- pasted text is inlined into the user message exactly as if typed; grepping every transcript in ~/.claude/projects/ for paste markers returns nothing. The host does not know, so no hook reading the host can know. WHAT WORKS: when the user pastes an agent reply, that text is usually ALREADY in the corpus as an earlier turn's assistant_summary, because JARVIS captured it when it was produced. So provenance is recoverable by cross-referencing the capture stream against its own past: a user turn that repeats an EARLIER assistant turn was not composed now. Implementation is 8-word hashed shingles (word-level survives the reformatting a paste picks up, where substring matching does not) plus a streaming index. THREE PROPERTIES BEAT THE FLAG THAT CANNOT BE BUILT: it works RETROACTIVELY over all existing records where a new field would only describe future ones; it is HOST-INDEPENDENT because Codex and Antigravity turns land in the same queue; and it is grounded in a FACT (this text existed before) rather than a judgement about style. DIRECTION IS THE WHOLE MEASUREMENT -- scoring against ALL turns instead of EARLIER ones reports 100% echo for the user's own repeated --ask question, because the answer quotes the question back; six such records topped the first run and none was a paste. ECHO_CEILING=0.30 is the measured precision knee (2/2 above 0.30; 4/7 above 0.15, and the 0.15-0.30 band is a real phenomenon -- answering a numbered list point by point reuses the assistant's vocabulary). VALIDATION THAT MATTERS MOST: it caught a row my own hand-labelling had marked GOOD -- 2026-09-06T00:06, which says 'I edited section 7 of that file two hours ago and wrote KB 527'. The user did not do that; I did. My own text pasted back, invisible to the grammar gate AND to a careful human read, found only by the corpus cross-reference. GENERALISES: when a stylistic signal cannot separate two classes, look for a FACTUAL one in data you already hold, and check whether the host records the ground truth before designing around the assumption that it does.

UNTRACKED jarvis_data/chromadb/ (2026-09-11), REVERSING a decision recorded one day earlier. The prior line said 'chromadb/ stays tracked anyway -- a 22 MB regenerable index isn't worth committing OR worth ripping out mid-project.' That was defensible when written and was obsoleted by a NEW FACT, not by a better opinion: the hearth's scheduler runs reindex_memory on a 12-hour cadence and is intended to run on BOTH machines. chroma.sqlite3 is a 23 MB binary and .gitattributes marks *.sqlite3 binary, so it has NO merge driver -- two machines rewriting it on a clock produces an unresolvable binary conflict the first time both sides commit. merge=union rescues *.jsonl only. The trigger was the user asking 'can we turn the hearth on here and in antigravity and in codex too?' -- a question about topology that surfaced a latent data-integrity hazard nobody had connected to it. WHAT MADE THE REVERSAL SAFE, and the part that is the actual lesson: I TESTED the regeneration claim before removing 23 MB from version control, instead of trusting the sentence I myself had written the day before. Ran scripts/ingest.py against a real tracked PDF with JARVIS_ROOT pointed at a scratch directory -> 99 embeddings in 18.5s, so all 24 tracked PDFs rebuild in ~8 minutes; index_memory.py for jarvis_memory was already proven by repeated use. This mattered because the SAME claim about this SAME directory had already been wrong twice in opposite directions -- first 'research_papers is not regenerable because the PDFs are gitignored' (false, all 24 are tracked), then 'stays tracked anyway'. Two wrong claims about one directory, neither of which survived anyone actually running the command. DIRECTIVE: a decision may be reversed when a NEW FACT changes the calculus -- that is not churn, it is the system working -- but say WHICH fact changed and leave the prior reasoning visible rather than overwriting it, so the next reader can tell a reversal from a flip-flop. And before deleting or untracking anything on the grounds that it is 'regenerable', RUN THE REGENERATION COMMAND ONCE against a scratch target. A regeneration path that has never been executed is a hypothesis, not a backup.

SECOND UNDECLARED-DEPENDENCY FIND, AND THE FIRST ONE'S DIRECTIVE DID NOT PREVENT IT (2026-09-11). uvicorn and pydantic are imported DIRECTLY by JARVIS code -- serve/hearth.py::serve() does a hard 'import uvicorn'; agent/tool.py and agent/state.py import pydantic at MODULE level -- and NEITHER was in requirements.txt. Nothing had ever failed on this machine because both arrive as TRANSITIVE dependencies of chromadb, so the gap was invisible to every test, every run, and every self-test. CAUGHT ONLY BECAUSE THE DOCS CHANGED: NERVOUS_SYSTEM.md and AGENTS.md had just started instructing a NEW machine to run 'python3 scripts/hearth.py --background' as a first-run step. That instruction would have failed on a clean venv -- the newly-written migration guide contained a command that could not work on the machine it was written for. The audit that found it was 'grep every third-party import across scripts/ and jarvis_core, diff against requirements.txt', which takes seconds and had never been run. WHY THIS IS THE SECOND INSTANCE: bashlex (KB, 2026-09-10) was the same failure exactly one day earlier -- imported directly by agent/bash_classifier.py, undeclared, and its absence soft-failed the permission gate to ASK on every command. That entry's directive was written and did not generalize, because it was phrased as a fact about bashlex rather than as a check to run. CLASSIFICATION: a transitive dependency is a COINCIDENCE, not a contract. The package that supplies it can drop it in any minor release, and the failure then appears on a machine nobody was testing, in a code path the tests do not cover (serve() is not exercised by hearth's own smoke tests, which test the ASGI app object rather than binding). DIRECTIVE, phrased as an executable check rather than a fact: before shipping any setup instruction, and after adding any import, run the import-vs-requirements diff -- ast-parse every .py under scripts/ and jarvis_core, collect non-stdlib top-level module names, and diff against requirements.txt. Declare everything you import DIRECTLY even when something else already pulls it in. Genuinely optional imports stay undeclared but must be listed in a comment block saying so, or the next audit re-flags them as oversights.

A TEST THAT LOOKED ISOLATED SILENTLY READ AND ALMOST WROTE REAL PRODUCTION STATE (found 2026-09-10, building the Codex capture adapter's self-test). Four functions used the pattern 'def f(path: Path = MODULE_CONSTANT)' -- find_rollouts(root=SESSIONS_ROOT), load_thread_names(path=SESSION_INDEX_PATH), read_watermark(path=WATERMARK_PATH), advance_watermark(fname, ts, path=WATERMARK_PATH). THE BUG: a default ARGUMENT VALUE is evaluated ONCE, at function-definition time, and baked into the function object -- it is NOT looked up fresh from the module's globals on each call. So the test's 'import ingest_codex_sessions as mod; mod.SESSIONS_ROOT = tempdir; mod.WATERMARK_PATH = tempfile' had NO EFFECT on find_rollouts()/read_watermark()/advance_watermark() called with no explicit path argument -- they kept using the REAL ~/.codex/sessions/ and the REAL jarvis_data/.codex_ingest_watermark.jsonl, baked in when the module first executed. HOW IT WAS CAUGHT: the test asserted 'run() ingests 2 exchanges from the synthetic session' and got 0 -- because it was silently reading the REAL watermark, which (from an earlier real run in the same session) had already advanced past both real rollouts' timestamps, so every real exchange looked already-ingested. WHY IT WAS NOT WORSE: if that real watermark had NOT already covered everything, the same bug would have caused the 'offline' test to APPEND SYNTHETIC TEST DATA into the real observation_queue.jsonl and silently ADVANCE the real ingestion watermark -- a test corrupting production state while reporting green. Verified after the fact: queue stayed at 599 lines, watermark unchanged; no corruption occurred, but only by chance of ordering. FIX: changed every such signature to 'param: Optional[Path] = None' with 'param = Path(param) if param is not None else MODULE_CONSTANT' as the FIRST LINE OF THE BODY -- a plain name reference inside a function body IS looked up fresh from the module's globals on every call, unlike a default argument value. This preserves identical external behavior (call with no args -> real path) while making module-level monkeypatching in tests actually take effect. DIRECTIVE: never use a mutable module-level path/constant as a parameter's DEFAULT VALUE if that path might ever need to be swapped for testing -- resolve it inside the function body instead. Grep for 'def .*: Path = [A-Z_]+\)' across the repo's other adapters (capture.py, recall.py, tension.py) as a follow-up; none were audited for this specific pattern today.

On three of them it wrote the id as 'PRIOR 429' rather than '429' -- echoing the '[PRIOR 429]' label MY OWN PROMPT used to present the priors. Exact match rejected those as hallucinations, so a working detector looked 60% unreliable and its true-positive rate was silently cut by more than half. TWO FIXES, both needed: (1) the prompt now labels priors '[id=429]' and asks for the id 'exactly as it appears after id=, digits only'; (2) _match_prior normalises before comparing -- strips a leading PRIOR/KB/entry/id token, brackets and whitespace, then falls back to a digit extraction that only resolves when EXACTLY ONE prior matches. The guard is not weakened: an id never shown still resolves to None (asserted by T13f). Stability after the fix: gold positive 5/5, hard negative 3/3. THIRD INSTRUMENTATION LESSON IN TWO DAYS: ScanReport now counts 'discarded (uncitable prior)' SEPARATELY from 'judge said NONE', because conflating them is exactly how a 60% suppression rate hid inside a plausible-looking zero. DIRECTIVE: a validator that rejects malformed-but-correct output is a false-negative generator, and it fails silently by construction. When a guard drops something, COUNT the drops as their own category -- never fold them into the legitimate-negative bucket. And check whether your own prompt's formatting is what the model is echoing back.

A SECURITY-RELEVANT DEPENDENCY WAS UNDECLARED, AND ITS ABSENCE WAS INVISIBLE (found 2026-09-10 by a regression run). agent/bash_classifier.py parses shell commands into a bashlex AST to decide ALLOW vs ASK vs DENY for shell_run -- it is part of the shipped permission gate. was NOT in requirements.txt and was not installed anywhere on disk. WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: the module soft-fails correctly (bash_classifier.py:174 -- ), so nothing broke, nothing warned, and no security hole opened. The ONLY symptom was ONE smoke test flipping (permgate 13/13 -> 12/13, 'T3 shell safe ALLOW' getting ASK). Everything else -- boot, the gate, --ask -- kept working while the classifier had silently degraded to 'ask about every command', which destroys exactly the precision it exists to provide. IMPORTANT CALIBRATION: this is a CAPABILITY loss, not a safety regression. The failure direction is conservative (ASK, never ALLOW), which is the correct design. But 'fails safe' is not the same as 'fails visibly', and a permission classifier that quietly stops classifying is a real defect. FIX: installed bashlex==0.18 and declared it in requirements.txt with the consequence written next to it. DIRECTIVE: when a component soft-fails on a missing optional import, the import MUST be declared as a hard dependency if the component is security-relevant -- and the degraded mode should announce itself, not merely be documented. Grep for across the safety layer and check each one is either declared or loudly reported.

ONE CLASSIFIER, TWO CONSUMERS, TWO MEANINGS OF THE SAME LABEL -- caught by the Final Boss (2026-09-09). Fixing the abstention conflation, I hard-coded domain_classifier.py's below-threshold fallback from 'general' to UNKNOWN. Correct for the ACTIVITY-domain consumer, where 'general' had no prototype and was pure abstention. But brain/router.py COMPOSES the same DomainClassifier with its own ROUTING prototypes, and there 'general' IS A REAL DESTINATION -- the general model pool, present in ROUTING_LABELS and mapped in _ROUTE_MAP. Abstaining in routing legitimately means 'send it to the general pool'. So my change made the router return a label outside its own vocabulary and the 50-query frozen gate fell below 80%: FINAL BOSS 7/8, leg 3 FAILED. Caught only because that harness exists and was re-run. FIX: fallback_label is now a per-consumer constructor argument (default UNKNOWN); the router passes fallback_label='general' with the reason written at the call site. Better than reverting -- it keeps the honesty fix where abstention really is abstention, and keeps the routing semantics where it is not. Final Boss restored 8/8. DIRECTIVE: before changing a SENTINEL VALUE in a shared component, enumerate the consumers and ask what that value MEANS to each one. A label can be an abstention in one caller and a legitimate category in another; the same string is not the same semantics. Grep for construction sites, not just for the constant.

A LONG QUERY RETRIEVES NEIGHBOURS, NOT THE THING IT CONTRADICTS (found + fixed 2026-09-09; this single fix was the difference between the detector finding nothing and working). The tension detector passed the WHOLE candidate entry as the retrieval query. Measured on the gold pair (KB 461 genuinely contradicts KB 429, confirmed by hand in KB 463): query = the full 1126-char entry -> 429 NOT IN THE TOP 15; query = its first 300 chars -> 429 at rank 9; query = one focused topic phrase -> 429 at rank 1, three times. CAUSE: a long entry covers several subjects, so its embedding is the AVERAGE of all of them and matches nothing sharply. It retrieves its own neighbours IN TIME (adjacent KB ids written the same day) rather than the specific decision it clashes with. Worse, the candidate's top TWO hits were ITSELF -- an entry is always its own strongest match, burning retrieval budget on a guaranteed non-prior. FIX: split the candidate into ~320-char overlapping windows (max 5), retrieve for each, union and dedupe; plus exclude the candidate's own entry_id explicitly rather than relying on the timestamp filter. RESULT: 461->429, 518->509 and 494->491 all now retrieve their true prior AT RANK 1, and the full pipeline (retrieval + judge, no hand-feeding) surfaces the 461/429 contradiction at 0.95 while staying silent on 518. WHAT THIS ALMOST HID: the first 30-day replay reported '0 findings'. The eval harness had passed 5/5 because I HAND-FED it the priors, so it measured the judge and not retrieval. DIRECTIVE: an eval that supplies its own inputs measures only the last stage. Instrument every stage of the funnel, and when a pipeline reports zero, prove WHICH stage produced the zero before believing it.

ABSTENTION HAD NO LABEL, AND THAT -- NOT THE SUBSTRING BUG -- WAS THE ROOT CAUSE (found + fixed 2026-09-09, on the user's insistence). The user rejected my proposed fix outright: 'I need a permanent solution, if we keep implementing better keyword matching it will result in the same bad labels that will silently kill the training corpus.' Correct, and investigating why produced a sharper diagnosis than I had. MEASURED ROOT CAUSE: guess_domain seeded best='general' and returned it on zero matches, so 'this turn is genuinely general' and 'I have no idea' were THE SAME TOKEN. Measured on the live queue: 309 of 583 records (53%) were labelled general, and ALL 309 had ZERO keyword hits -- not one was a positive classification. An abstention was literally unrepresentable, which is why 99 days and ~15% wrong labels went unnoticed. THE TRAP I ALMOST WALKED INTO: agent/domain_classifier.py, the embedding classifier built precisely BECAUSE keywords failed, ALSO fell back to 'general' below threshold. Swapping keywords for embeddings alone would have been more accurate and equally undiagnosable. THE FIX IS FOUR PROPERTIES, only the first about accuracy: (1) semantic not lexical; (2) UNKNOWN as a distinct outcome, never 'general' -- this converts an invisible failure into a counted one; (3) the cosine SCORE persisted next to every label so a wrong threshold is inspectable; (4) a 28-turn hand-labelled GOLD SET wired into check_projections.py, which already runs on the scheduler. Property 4 is what makes it permanent: any classifier drifts as the work moves, so the durable property is not being right today but SAYING WHEN IT STOPS BEING RIGHT. The gate proved itself immediately -- first run scored 68%, refused to pass, and its misses showed the prototypes had no seeds for AWS Glue, VACUUM, ADF, SFT or RunPod. Adding seeds for that real vocabulary: 89%. DIRECTIVE: any classifier that cannot say 'I do not know' will hide its own failure rate forever. Give abstention its own label before tuning anything else.

THE SURFACING DETECTOR WAS REPLACED, NOT TUNED (2026-09-09). agent/tension.py supersedes correlation.py's link-proposal path. WHY REPLACEMENT WAS THE ONLY OPTION, all three measured: (1) The old detector could only fire when a domain DECLINED (vol_drop <=> b_recent < 0.6*b_earlier). The numerator grows with every captured turn; the denominator is a frozen slice of history. So its ability to say ANYTHING decayed monotonically toward zero the more JARVIS was used -- ANTI-INDUCTIVE, the exact opposite of what a memory organ should be. Replaying the real queue: 75 turns -> 1 candidate, 115 turns -> 0, and _deterministic_confidence was never called even once, so the 0.60 floor rejected nothing. (2) Its output was never a memory: lifetime total three sentences, all 2026-06-18, all restating one volume shift. (3) Its 'confidence' was a hand-rolled weighted sum with a free 0.35 base capped at 0.70 -- every shipped insight read '70%' because that was the cap. WHAT REPLACED IT: candidate = what the user is doing now (KB appends AND verbatim observation_queue turns); corpus = their own 305 Decision/Failure/Cognitive_Pattern entries via the EXISTING chromadb index (no re-index -- entry_type/timestamp metadata was already there); output = a RELATION (REVERSES/REPEATS/RECONFUSES/NONE) against a NAMED prior, fail-closed to NONE on every error path. Reuses ContradictionJudge's discipline from brain/reasoning.py rather than inventing a second judge. DIRECTIVE: when a detector's gate becomes harder to satisfy as data accumulates, that is a design fault, not a tuning problem -- check the monotonicity of every threshold against volume before shipping it.

ROW 0b MEASURED AND IT IS NEGATIVE: THE FLOOR IS NOT THE BOTTLENECK (2026-09-08). The scheduler now runs the consolidator every 6h, and it ran three times today, each exiting ok. New life-state feed entries produced: ZERO. The feed still holds 3 insights, all from 2026-06-18, and life_state_monitor --peek still says '(nothing to surface)'. Measured cause via consolidate.py --dry-run: window=21d turns=115 domains=5 **links=0** floor=0.6. Compare the same command on 2026-09-06: 75 turns, 5 domains, 1 link at 0.592. So the corpus grew 75 -> 115 turns and the number of candidate links went 1 -> 0. TWO CONCLUSIONS, both load-bearing. (1) The 0.60 confidence floor is NOT the binding constraint. I had framed it as 'links cross the floor as the queue grows' and expected 0.592 to rise -- instead there is now nothing at ANY confidence. Lowering the floor would surface nothing, because CrossDomainCorrelationEngine finds no cross-domain relationship to score. (2) The plumbing was never the gate. Steps 2-7 fixed the pulse (a Stop hook, then a real clock), and the pulse is now demonstrably independent of the user opening --ask -- and the organ STILL has nothing to say. stage_6_integration/ROADMAP.md 6.10 already states the correct gate: 'ambient presence is worth exactly as much as the surfacing organ has to say... build 6.10 only after the organ demonstrably produces insights worth interrupting someone for -- measured, not assumed.' It is now measured. DIRECTIVE: before any further ambient/delivery work (step 8 Telegram push included), the open question is whether domain-volume correlation is the wrong detector for 'what did I forget', not whether the transport reaches the user. Building a push channel for an organ that emits nothing would be the most expensive way yet to learn this.

PYTHON GOTCHA that silently breaks log-grepping: on a str-mixin Enum, str(x) and f-string formatting DISAGREE. PermissionDecision is declared 'class PermissionDecision(str, Enum)' with DENY = 'deny'. Then: str(P.DENY) -> 'PermissionDecision.DENY' (Enum.__str__ wins), f'{P.DENY}' -> 'deny' (the str mixin supplies __format__, and f-strings call __format__ not __str__), repr(P.DENY) -> "<PermissionDecision.DENY: 'deny'>". Cost me a false test failure: the code logged the decision with an f-string ('deny') while the assertion searched for the str() form ('PermissionDecision.DENY'). The real hazard is not tests -- it is that a log line written one way and grepped the other NEVER matches, and a monitoring rule built on it silently never fires. DIRECTIVE: when logging an enum whose value must be machine-matched later, use repr() or .value explicitly, never bare interpolation. Fixed in Python 3.11+ for IntEnum via __str__ changes, but this repo runs 3.10 and the str-mixin case remains divergent regardless.

TWO DEFECTS IN THE SCHEDULER THAT BOTH LOOKED LIKE SUCCESS (2026-09-08, both caught by running it rather than testing it). (1) STAGGER SILENCED THE ONE-SHOT. Jobs carry initial_delay_seconds to avoid a thundering herd at daemon boot. hearth.py --tick-once builds a fresh Scheduler, so started_at is now, so EVERY job reported 'not due' -- the command printed 'ran: nothing was due' and did nothing, every time, while exiting 0. Fixed with tick(ignore_stagger=True); interval cadence still honoured so a one-shot cannot force a needless reindex. (2) A SHARED GUARD LET ONE JOB CLEAR ANOTHER'S. Both refresh_profile and reindex_memory guarded on the SAME command, scripts/check_projections.py, which exits non-zero if ANY projection is stale. Measured live: refresh_profile ran first, fixed the two projections it owns, and reindex_memory then saw exit 0 and recorded 'skipped -- guard reports nothing to do'. So the vector index would NEVER be rebuilt regardless of how far it drifted, and the skip counter would keep reporting healthy. Fixed by adding --only SUBSTRING to check_projections so each job guards on the artifact IT can fix. DIRECTIVE: a guard shared between two fixers is not a guard -- scope every conditional job to the exact artifact it repairs. And both of these are the DECORATIVE-CODE class again (tests pass, position makes it inert): the only way either surfaced was executing the real thing and reading what it actually did.

I SWITCHED A READER BEFORE MIGRATING ITS DATA, AND IMMEDIATELY BROKE THE GUARANTEE I WAS PROTECTING (2026-09-08, self-inflicted, caught within one command). Changing the life-state watermark from .surfaced_watermark (JSON) to .surfaced_watermark.jsonl (append-only log) was correct. But I edited the code first and left the new .jsonl EMPTY, so surfaced_ids() returned an empty set and the very next invocation re-surfaced insight 5b17b2bebd4e -- an insight already shown on 2026-06-18. That is exactly the 'NEVER NAG: each insight surfaces AT MOST ONCE, ever' guarantee the change existed to make durable. Nothing was lost (the feed was untouched and the re-surface reached me, not the user) and I folded the 3 legacy ids into the new log, which collapsed the accidental duplicate. DIRECTIVE: when relocating a store, the order is MIGRATE THE DATA, THEN SWITCH THE READER -- never the reverse. A reader pointed at an empty new location does not fail loudly; it reports 'nothing recorded yet', which is indistinguishable from a clean slate and silently voids every guarantee built on that record. Same shape as the index_memory tier-metadata bug (1030 chunks, 0 hits, looked like success).

THE TORN-LINE APPEND DEFECT: a flock does NOT make an append-only log safe (found 2026-09-08 by a test written for unrelated new code). A lock serialises concurrent writers. It does nothing about a writer that was KILLED mid-write, which leaves a final line with no newline terminator -- and the NEXT append then lands on that same line, so the torn record DESTROYS the good record appended after it rather than only itself. A fold over the log then loses both. Discovered because a smoke test wrote a corrupt watermark as '}{corrupt' with no trailing newline and the good event appended after it vanished; the assertion I expected to be trivially true failed. Audit result: kb_append.py has guarded this since it shipped ('Ensure we start on a fresh line even if the file lacked a trailing \n' -- seek SEEK_END, read the last byte, write \n if needed), and THREE other append-only logs had never copied it: agent/capture.py append_observation (the observation queue, written every single turn), agent/context_ledger.py archive_span (where a lost span makes an evicted context unrecoverable -- it defeats that module's entire purpose), and agent/life_state_monitor.py mark_surfaced. All three fixed; suites 18/18, 17/17, 20/20. DIRECTIVE: every append-only writer must heal a missing terminator BEFORE appending. The correct pattern already existed in this repo and three later call sites diverged from it -- when a subtle correctness guard exists in one place, grep for the other writers rather than assuming the idiom spread.

BOTH DEFERRED STEP-6 ITEMS RE-EXAMINED AND BOTH OF MY ORIGINAL RATIONALES WERE WRONG (2026-09-08). I had deferred content-addressed KB ids and the watermark event-fold with one sentence: 'both solve concurrent multi-writer conflicts that cannot exist until the hearth ships.' Measured before building: (1) CONTENT-ADDRESSED IDS -- the motivating L303 collision has NEVER OCCURRED. kb_append.py --audit over 558 entries with 258 explicit ids returns duplicate_ids {}. fcntl.flock plus single-user-at-a-time held for the file's whole life, and the hearth does NOT add a same-machine writer flock cannot serialise. So a risky rewrite of the widest-reach field in the repo (five consumers read id) would have prevented a failure with no instances. Replaced with a DETECTOR: projections.id_collisions() + a check_projections line. (2) WATERMARK -- mark_surfaced was ALREADY flock'd with a correct read-modify-write, so same-machine concurrency was never the hazard either. The real hazard was git: .surfaced_watermark was a TRACKED JSON object, and JSON has no union merge driver, so two laptops surfacing insights clobber each other's ids -- which breaks the never-nag guarantee this file exists to keep. Fix was smaller and better than an event-fold format: rename to .surfaced_watermark.jsonl and it inherits merge=union from .gitattributes for free. Concatenation IS merge. DIRECTIVE: 'defer until X exists' is only valid if X is VERIFIED to be the thing that creates the condition. I asserted the hearth would create the writers; flock already handled the same-machine case and git had already created the cross-machine case months earlier. Verify the precondition, not just the fix.

HEARTH v0 SHIPPED (2026-09-08, omnipresence step 7). jarvis_core/serve/hearth.py + scheduler.py: ONE always-on process owns the mutable state and the clock; every surface becomes a socket client. Raw ASGI, NOT FastAPI -- uvicorn 0.46 is already installed while fastapi/starlette are absent, so this adds ZERO dependencies, and a bare ASGI callable is testable with a fake receive/send pair with no socket at all (all 23 hearth tests run offline). Verified live: POST /v1/ask boots the real Mind, calls 4-9 tools, streams narration over SSE, and a SECOND request continued the same conversation session -- 'same mind' is now a routing property, not a sync problem. Safety posture is deliberately timid: binds 127.0.0.1 only AND re-checks the peer address per request, requires a bearer token even on loopback (loopback is not a boundary against other local processes), serialises to one request at a time with 409 rather than interleaving mutable session state, and DENIES every permission prompt while reporting the denial in the response. DIRECTIVE: --ask keeps its in-process default and gains opt-in --via-hearth, because the hearth has no TTY so it cannot honour a human gate -- routing the terminal there by default would SILENTLY REDUCE capability. That flips to default once the Commitment gate (step 10) provides remote approval.

STEP 6 NARROWED, AND TWO OF ITS THREE PARTS WERE PREMATURE (2026-09-08). Investigating step 6 produced three findings that shrank it, and I reported rather than executed the original scope. FINDING 1 -- I HAD MY OWN DIAGNOSIS WRONG. I called the 544-vs-533 gap 'the mind disagrees with itself'. It was real but it SELF-HEALS: profile_synth.py rebuilds the index whenever it runs, and all three artifacts now read 557. It was never a fork, it was a STALENESS WINDOW that opens on every KB append and closes on the next regeneration. So the defect was never that projections go wrong -- it is that NOTHING LOOKS. I found it by accident, and accident is not a detection strategy. FINDING 2 -- parts 1 and 3 fix a conflict that cannot occur yet. Content-addressing KB ids fixes the L303 collision (kb_append._next_id is max(ids,300)+1, so two machines mint the same id) and the watermark event-fold buys multi-device merge safety. But CLAUDE.md:58 states the operating model: 'Single-user-at-a-time -- no concurrent edits.' Concurrent writers do not exist until the hearth does (step 7), and part 1 has the widest blast radius in the repo -- search_memory, kb_compact, cognitive_index, profile_synth and the new index_memory all read id. Deferred to step 7, where the writers actually appear. FINDING 3, AND IT CHANGED THE DESIGN RATHER THAN THE TIMING -- 'demote projections out of git' WOULD HAVE BROKEN THE PERSONAL LAPTOP. cognitive_profile.md and activity_digest.md are projections AND ALSO THE SYNC TRANSPORT: js-workspace-rule.md:21-22 tells that machine to READ both at boot, and line 25 records why it cannot rebuild them -- 'there is NO per-prompt capture here (Antigravity has no hook system)'. No local queue means no digest. Untracking them looks like obvious cleanup and blinds the other machine. So KB 548's taxonomy gains a third class: FACT (authoritative, tracked) / PROJECTION (derived, rebuildable WHERE READ, untracked) / PROJECTION-AS-TRANSPORT (derived here, consumed by a machine that CANNOT rebuild it, tracked and correctly so). ALSO VERIFIED FALSE: CLAUDE.md:123 claimed ChromaDB 'never committed' and pointed at scripts/sync_chromadb.py for regeneration. ChromaDB IS committed (17 files, 19MB) and that script DOES NOT EXIST -- wrong on both counts, the sixth prose-vs-code instance this week. And untracking chromadb is unsafe: research_papers' 156 embeddings cannot be regenerated because the source PDFs are gitignored too. SHIPPED: jarvis_core/brain/projections.py (14/14) as the core organ -- I first wrote the logic in scripts/ and corrected it, since this repo's contract is core organ + thin adapter; scripts/check_projections.py is now the CLI, exit 1 on stale so it works from a hook or CI rather than only for a human who remembered to look. Registered as a boot-inhale provider that returns None when healthy, so a clean system costs ZERO prompt tokens and only a real problem speaks. Untracked cognitive_index.sqlite3 and behavioral_state_model.jsonl; asserted the transport artifacts are still tracked, because that is the plausible-looking mistake. PROVEN: appended a KB entry without regenerating -> both zero-tolerance projections reported STALE at (-1) with the fix command and exit 1; ran profile_synth -> green, exit 0. Regression: projections 14/14, context_injector 18/18, boot 20/20, react 112/112, compact 18/18, Final Boss 8/8. DIRECTIVE: this is the THIRD instrument of the same family -- usage.py (row 0), the life_state feed (row 0b), projections.py (integrity). Each exists because something true about the system was UNREPRESENTABLE: no row, no counter, no delta, therefore unnoticeable. When something matters and nothing counts it, add the counter before adding the feature.

STEP 5 SHIPPED: MEMORY NOW ARRIVES UNPROMPTED — the moat mechanism works for the first time (2026-09-08). MemoryManager (928 lines, 51 tests) had ZERO production construction sites, so react.py's auto-retrieve branch was unreachable on every real --ask and memory reached the prompt ONLY when the model chose to call a tool. That is verbatim ENDGAME Sec1.2's failure: 'it cannot fire when you did not know to ask.' TWO PREREQUISITES HAD TO LAND FIRST AND I NEARLY SHIPPED WITHOUT EITHER. (1) THERE WAS NOTHING TO RETRIEVE. Measured: ChromaDB held exactly ONE collection, research_papers, 156 embeddings. The knowledge base, conversations and observation queue were NOT indexed at all. Wiring auto_retrieve_top_k>0 that day would have auto-retrieved RESEARCH PAPERS and LOOKED LIKE THE FEATURE WORKED — the most dangerous possible outcome. This is boot.py's own founding L324 bug still live: 'asked what have we built, searched one ChromaDB collection of research papers and honestly found nothing, while knowledge_base.jsonl sat unread.' The 2026 fix then was prior_self_consult as a TOOL, which is exactly why memory required asking. Built scripts/index_memory.py: streams the KB, renders type+tags+content so a hit carries provenance, chunks via the existing RecursiveWordChunker (900/180, respecting MiniLM's 256-token ceiling per KB 508), upserts by deterministic id into a new jarvis_memory collection. (2) A SECOND, INVISIBLE PREREQUISITE: metadata.tier. MemoryManager.retrieve queries with where={'tier': tier.value}, so records lacking that field are invisible. 1030 correctly-indexed chunks returned ZERO hits until tagged tier='warm'. WARM is right, not HOT — HOT is an in-process LRU that dies with the process; the KB is durable and semantically searchable. A THIRD BUG FOUND BY DISBELIEVING A PLAUSIBLE NUMBER: the first dry-run reported 254 entries against a 554-line KB. Cause: the KB has TWO SCHEMA GENERATIONS — 250 entries carry uid=1000(swara_unix) gid=1000(swara_unix) groups=1000(swara_unix),4(adm),20(dialout),24(cdrom),25(floppy),27(sudo),29(audio),30(dip),44(video),46(plugdev),117(netdev) (plus source_machine), 281 older ones carry only content/expiry/tags/timestamp/type. Keying on uid=1000(swara_unix) gid=1000(swara_unix) groups=1000(swara_unix),4(adm),20(dialout),24(cdrom),25(floppy),27(sudo),29(audio),30(dip),44(video),46(plugdev),117(netdev) silently skipped 300 entries, 54% of the mind's memory, and '254' was plausible enough to pass. Fixed with stable_key(): uid=1000(swara_unix) gid=1000(swara_unix) groups=1000(swara_unix),4(adm),20(dialout),24(cdrom),25(floppy),27(sudo),29(audio),30(dip),44(video),46(plugdev),117(netdev) when present, else a content hash — now 554 entries / 1030 chunks. Same silent-partial-coverage class as KB 508. VERIFIED, and the isolation matters: with ZERO tools available so nothing COULD be asked for, the assembled system prompt already contained 'tier=WARM score=0.05 id=kb-538-1' verbatim including the exact constant _DEFAULT_BUDGET_USD. Memory arrives BEFORE the model gets a turn. Wired in boot.py only when a store is open (no store -> no WARM tier -> auto-retrieve would burn a query per turn for nothing); _AUTO_RETRIEVE_TOP_K=4 because every item is a standing per-turn token tax, not a one-off. Regression: memory_manager 51/51, react 112/112, mind 15/15, boot 20/20, permgate 13/13, compact 18/18, Final Boss 8/8. HONEST CAVEAT ON ROW 0b: a live --ask still ALSO called prior_self_consult, so the strict acceptance test ('no memory tool in the call list') did not pass — the model has a tool it likes and will keep using it. What is proven is that the unprompted channel now works and reaches the prompt first. Whether it makes JARVIS say the thing you did not ask for is the measurement that remains, and index_memory.py must be RE-RUN as the KB grows or retrieval silently goes stale. STEP 4 SHIPPED: THE CONTEXT LEDGER — eviction is now REVERSIBLE (2026-09-08). New organs: agent/context_ledger.py (17/17 tests) + agent/tools/context.py ContextExpandTool (10/10). Compaction was a one-way door: compact.py replaced a window with a summary and persisted the originals NOWHERE. Now every span is archived VERBATIM to an append-only flock'd JSONL under jarvis_data/context/<session>.jsonl BEFORE eviction, keyed by a content-addressed handle (sha256[:16]), and the boundary message carries ctx:<handle> so the transcript itself points back at what it dropped. If the archive write FAILS the compaction is ABANDONED — a smaller prompt is not worth an unrecoverable transcript. Handles double as checksums: expand_span verifies the content still hashes to its own handle and returns None on mismatch, so corruption is detectable rather than served as plausible-looking wrong history. TWO DISCOVERIES THAT CHANGED THE DESIGN, both found by tests I wrote to prove the opposite. (1) A FORMAT MISMATCH silently disabled the whole anti-drift mechanism: as_message() emitted a BARE handle inside context_expand(...), while extract_handles() only matches the ctx: prefixed form. Writer and reader disagreed, so _resolve_originals could never find a prior boundary. Caught only because the two-pass drift test asserted on the summariser's actual INPUT rather than on a return flag. (2) THE ANTI-DRIFT LAW WAS ALREADY SATISFIED STRUCTURALLY, and my defence was aimed at the wrong risk. A boundary carries role='system' and is inserted immediately after the lead, so _split() classifies it as LEADING on the next pass and it never re-enters a compactable window — a summary can therefore never be summarised. But that exposed a REAL problem I had not designed for: boundaries then ACCUMULATE in the lead, which is never compacted, so ten compactions would leave ten permanently-resident summaries and a prompt floor that creeps up forever. Fixed by folding: _split_lead separates prior boundaries, _expand_boundaries expands their handles back to originals, and the new summary is computed from THAT union — so exactly ONE boundary survives at any time AND derivation depth stays 1. Proven over three successive compactions: boundaries stayed at 1, the third summary read ORIG-0 and contained no prior SUMMARY text, and accounting was exact — 16 archived + 2 resident = all 18 originals, zero gaps, zero double-counting. An unexpandable handle KEEPS its boundary rather than dropping the only trace of it. WIRED IN PRODUCTION: assemble_mind gained session_id, builds the ledger once and shares it between the compactor and the tool; orchestrator passes sess.session_id. Verified live: --ask now ships 6 tools including context_expand, compactor._ledger is a ContextLedger, path keyed per session. permgate allowlists context_expand as read-only (it reads one append-only file by handle and cannot write). ALSO corrected permgate's docstring, which still read 'default ALLOW for the safe majority' — accurate prose for the fail-open bug fixed in step 1, and the FIFTH instance this week of prose outliving the code it described. jarvis_data/context/ gitignored: machine-local working memory, not the mind. Regression: context_ledger 17/17, tools.context 10/10, compact 18/18, react 112/112, mind 15/15, tokens 21/21, boot 20/20, permgate 13/13, llm_client 23/23, context_injector 18/18, Final Boss 8/8. DIRECTIVE: 'infinite context' now means exactly this — nothing is unreachable, the model always knows what it is NOT looking at, and no byte is dropped without a marker saying how to get it back. Do not describe it as unbounded attention.

STEP 3: THE COMPACTOR WAS WIRED TO A POSITION WHERE IT COULD NOT POSSIBLY HELP (found + fixed 2026-09-08). Three defects, all verified, and the middle one is the interesting failure mode. (1) boot.py never passed compactor=, so Mind._compactor was None on every real --ask and WorkingMemoryCompactor -- 322 lines, 17 passing tests -- had NEVER executed outside its own smoke suite. (2) mind.py:191 called _maybe_compact(react) AFTER _run_react had already returned. By then every oversized request had already been sent, and the message list being compacted was about to be discarded with the run. Worse, mind.py:313 computed 'result = await compact(...)' and then returned bool(result.compacted), DROPPING result.messages. So even in its own tests the compaction was thrown away. (3) ReActLoop.__init__ had NO compactor parameter at all -- there was no seam to pass one through, so nothing could have wired it correctly without this change. THE CLASS OF BUG IS 'DECORATIVE CODE': not dead (it ran in tests, and MindResult.compacted was populated from it) but positioned so it cannot affect the outcome. That is harder to spot than dead code, because coverage and a green suite both look fine. FIX: added compactor= to ReActLoop, added ReActLoop._compact_in_place() which does 'messages[:] = result.messages' -- the assignment mind.py never made -- and called it BEFORE self._call_llm inside the iteration loop. ReActResult gained compactions:int. Mind now threads compactor= down and _maybe_compact is rewritten to a pure read (react.compactions > 0). boot.py constructs the compactor. A DESIGN ERROR I MADE AND CAUGHT MID-STEP: I first sized the compaction threshold from the model's context_length via TokenBudget. That looks right and is wrong -- google/gemini-3.6-flash reports context_length=1048576, so a window-sized threshold would never compact until ~1M tokens. OVERFLOW IS NOT THE BINDING PROBLEM; RE-BILLING IS: react.py:390 re-sends the whole transcript every iteration, so at max_iterations=40 a T-token prefix costs ~40*T. That is precisely why one hard question cost Rs72 on 2026-09-07. Corrected to a COST-driven target (_COMPACT_COST_TARGET_TOKENS = 48_000) with the real window allowed only to LOWER it -- verified: 1M-window model -> 48,000; an 8K model -> 5,952. PROVEN END TO END, asserting on the message list rather than a bool as the plan demanded: a scripted 7-iteration run with 4KB tool blobs produced compactions=4, the boundary summary present in the LIVE message list, and a correct final answer. Regression: react 112/112, mind 15/15, compact 17/17, tokens 21/21, memory_manager 51/51, boot 20/20, llm_client 23/23, permgate 13/13, context_injector 18/18, Final Boss 8/8. DIRECTIVE: when a component has passing tests but has never run in production, check WHERE it is called before assuming it works -- position is a correctness property, and 'it has tests' does not establish it.

STEP 2 SHIPPED: ONE CALIBRATED TOKEN COUNTER, REPLACING TWO len//4 GUESSES (2026-09-08). New organ agent/tokens.py — TokenCounter + TokenBudget + a process-wide shared_counter(). 21/21 smoke tests. WHAT WAS WRONG: every token number in the system was len(text)//4, in TWO independent copies that could drift — brain/llm_client.py:75 (used once at :225 for the budget gate) and agent/compact.py:73 + estimate_tokens() (used at :82 and :180 for every compaction decision). Worse, NOTHING anywhere compared an assembled prompt against the target model's context_length, even though that value is loaded at router.py:241 and llm_client.pick_free_model literally SORTS on it. So the system could not answer the question that governs all paging: will this fit? WHY NOT A TOKENIZER: tiktoken is not installed; transformers is, but the catalog holds 364 models across a dozen tokenizer families and loading one per model on CPU is not viable — and it would be a DIFFERENT wrong answer, since OpenAI BPE does not tokenize Gemini or Kimi text. THE BETTER SOURCE WAS ALREADY THERE: llm_client.py:264-266 reads usage.prompt_tokens from the provider response and only falls back to the estimate. Every real call is a free labelled sample — we sent N chars, the provider counted T tokens. observe(model, chars, actual) feeds that back via EWMA (alpha 0.25), so each model's ratio converges on measured reality with zero new dependencies. Guard rails: samples under 200 chars ignored as noise, ratios outside 1.5-12.0 ignored rather than absorbed (a poisoned ratio silently breaks every paging decision). ONE BUG I INTRODUCED AND CAUGHT: observe() was wired but save() was not, so calibration lived only in memory — and since every --ask is a fresh process, the ratio would have reset to 4.0 forever and never converged. Fixed with an atexit flush (one write per process, not one per observation). LIVE RESULT, and it is honestly deflating: after one real question (5 samples) google/gemini-3.6-flash learned 3.9639 chars/token — almost exactly the old hardcoded 4.0. The old guess was fine FOR THIS MODEL ON ENGLISH PROSE. The value is not that 4.0 was wrong, it is that it is now MEASURED PER MODEL, so code-heavy, CJK and Kimi-tokenizer models will diverge visibly instead of silently. ALSO: deleted llm_client's now-unreferenced _CHARS_PER_TOKEN outright rather than leaving it with a 'kept for tests' comment — CLAUDE.md forbids exactly that shim, and I had written one before checking. token_ratios.json is gitignored as a PROJECTION (KB 548 taxonomy); syncing it would repeat the cognitive_index/chromadb mistake that hid the 544-vs-533 drift. Regression: tokens 21/21, compact 17/17, react 112/112, llm_client 23/23, boot 20/20, memory_manager 51/51, permgate 13/13, context_injector 18/18, Final Boss 8/8. DIRECTIVE: TokenBudget is now the only sanctioned way to ask 'does this fit'; do not reintroduce a local chars-per-token constant anywhere.

THE PERMISSION GATE FAILED OPEN, AND ITS OWN ENGINE'S DOCSTRING SAID OTHERWISE (found + fixed 2026-09-08). agent/permissions.py:44-46 states 'Default is ASK -- the engine fails closed: if nothing matches and no classifier weighs in, a human must approve.' brain/permgate.py:106 built the LIVE context with default=PermissionDecision.ALLOW, inverting it. PROVEN ON THE REAL PRODUCTION TOOLSET, not inferred: build_permission_context(default_toolset()) returned ALLOW for 'shell_run' and ALLOW for the invented name 'a_new_tool_nobody_gated'. TWO DISTINCT FAIL-OPEN PATHS, both measured: (1) a tool ABSENT from the toolset when the context is built resolves to ALLOW -- shell_run ships only in full_toolset(), so on the default --ask path the gate positively permitted a tool it had never seen; (2) any NEW tool that forgets requires_permission=True is silently permitted, so safety depended on every future tool author remembering a boolean. This is an allowlist expressed as a denylist. FIX: added an explicit _READ_ONLY_TOOLS frozenset, emit ALLOW rules only for tools named there AND present, keep ASK rules for requires_permission tools, and invert the default to ASK. Polarity inverted, behaviour preserved: every tool the system actually ships is read-only and still resolves ALLOW, file_read's repo-scope classifier still ALLOWs in-repo paths and ASKs for /etc/passwd and ~/.bashrc, and memory_semantic_search resolves ALLOW once a store is open. What changed is only the unknown case: shell_run and a_new_tool_nobody_gated now reach the human. Regression clean: permgate 13/13, boot 20/20, react 112/112, permissions 30/30. STILL OPEN, deliberately not fixed in this pass: react.py:911-912 returns ALLOW when no permission context is wired -- NOT the production hole, because orchestrator.py:512 always builds one (p_ctx = permission_context or build_permission_context(prebuilt)), and 46 of 54 ReActLoop constructions are smoke tests that would break on a blind flip. And agent/executor.py has ZERO occurrences of 'permission' -- the DAG executor dispatches safe_invoke ungated; it must be gated or deleted before any effectful tool exists. DIRECTIVE: this is the FOURTH instance this week of prose-declares-X / code-does-not-X (KB 521 self-describing files, KB 527 prose status headers, 2026-09-06 privacy guarantee, KB 547 the gitignored-in-comment-only settings file). In this repo a policy stated only in prose is not merely unenforced -- it is routinely FALSE. When you read a docstring asserting a safety property, VERIFY IT AGAINST A LIVE CALL before relying on it.

CONNECTIVITY ARCHITECTURE DECISIONS + THE STORAGE/INDEX DISTINCTION (2026-09-08, user-confirmed across two turns). FIVE DECISIONS: (1) Third-party servers may call JARVIS -- wanted as a capability, not a near-term use. Shape is a SCOPED OUTBOUND TOKEN (ask:readonly, no tools, no memory writes, no spend), rate-limited, revocable, Intent-Ledger-logged, and deliberately the LAST build step because exposing a system whose permission layer currently fails open is the one thing that must not happen early. (2) The restaurant call STAYS -- I raised the objection once, the user overruled it, AND I WAS PARTLY WRONG: my objection was US-centric (California B.O.T. Act), and India has no bot-disclosure statute for a personal agent placing a call; TRAI's UCC framework governs MARKETING calls, not this. The objection is replaced by a REQUIREMENT: a call must end in verifiable confirmation (callback, SMS, booking reference) or report failure, because a booking wrongly believed successful is worse than none. (3) Device-key storage gets an interface NOW, implemented as a plain file -- free today, expensive after devices are enrolled. Host-compromise threat model deferred by the user until JARVIS is complete. (4) Telegram now -> browser PWA -> native Android with Firebase (free) + Play Store (one-time $25). iOS DROPPED: $99/yr is 38% of the conservative annual envelope, for one user, on an envelope with no hosting line. (5) GraphRAG 4.6 PROMOTED from trigger-gated-deferred to REQUIRED. THE CONCEPTUAL CORRECTION, which is the substantive content and fixes a live bug: the user asked 'context storage is GraphRAG, what about memory storage -- SQLite?' GraphRAG is NOT storage. It is one of four INDEXES. Storage = the append-only log (knowledge_base.jsonl + the new Context Ledger), authoritative, the only thing that is true. Indexes = ChromaDB (semantic), BM25 (keyword), cognitive_index.sqlite3 (structured), GraphRAG (multi-hop) -- all derived, disposable, rebuildable. This is ENDGAME Sec4's own 4-Layer Retrieval Stack, already written; the user's instinct pointed straight at their own architecture. THE LOG MUST STAY JSONL AND MUST NOT MOVE TO SQLITE: append-only JSONL has the property that CONCATENATION IS MERGE, which is the entire basis of the multi-device coherence design; a SQLite file is a binary B-tree and two devices writing it produce a conflict git cannot merge. LIVE BUG THIS EXPLAINS: KB 544 entries vs cognitive_index 533 vs cognitive_profile header 533, with ALL FIVE artifacts git-tracked INCLUDING the derived ones -- syncing a projection as if authoritative is how a mind forks on one machine unnoticed. WHY GRAPHRAG IS NOW REQUIRED: the Context Ledger delivers unbounded RECALL, but retrieval is query-shaped and cannot serve the one case of connecting two distant facts when you did not know to look for either -- which is multi-hop, is Layer 3's stated job, and is verbatim Sec1.2's moat sentence. DIRECTIVE: never again describe GraphRAG, Chroma, BM25 or SQLite as storage; they are indexes over one append-only log.

PRODUCTION DEFAULT IS THE CONFIGURATION ALREADY PROVEN UNRELIABLE -- with a live receipt (trial Entry 006, 2026-09-07). Asked 'what can you tell me about lakebase and pgbenchmark', --ask answered that 'pgbench (often referred to as pgbenchmark)' is the same tool. FACTUALLY WRONG: pgbenchmark is a distinct third-party PyPI package (Apache-2.0, Python>=3.10, 0.1.7.1 Apr 2025) that times a single query in a Python loop; pgbench is the official contrib concurrent load generator. The reasoning audit rated this SOUND [self-audit: google/gemini-3.6-flash] -- 'auditor re-derived independently and agrees'. KB L390-class finding (same-model critic unreliable) was already recorded 2026-06-17 and FIXED by the Wave-2 independent critic, BUT orchestrator.py:1629 documents critic_independent=False as THE PRODUCTION DEFAULT and --critic-model is opt-in, so the default --ask path still ships the known-bad configuration. This is the first instance of it false-SOUNDing a FACTUAL error rather than a reasoning error -- the prior evidence was all multi-turn reasoning, so factual claims were an untested surface. NOTE the epistemic layer that DID work: confidence correctly returned ESCALATE (0.24), best-evidence cosine 0.33, and the answer opened by stating neither term exists in the KB. So the system knew it was ignorant and said so; the audit line then overwrote that signal with unearned reassurance. DIRECTIVE: do not read 'reasoning audit: SOUND' as corroboration when the tag says self-audit -- it means only 'the same model agrees with itself'. Either pass --critic-model on questions whose answer is checkable, or stop printing SOUND for same-model audits at ESCALATE-level confidence.

PER-QUESTION SPEND CEILING REMOVED FROM --ask (2026-09-07, user directive). _DEFAULT_BUDGET_USD in brain/orchestrator.py goes 0.10 -> None. CostTracker, build_llm_call and RoutingConstraints already treated None as unbounded, so the mechanism supported this cleanly; only ONE site did arithmetic on the value -- the critic budget, round(budget_usd * 0.5) -- which now guards for None because halving None is not a smaller number, it is a crash. Type hints widened to Optional[float] at 3 orchestrator signatures plus OpenRouterTarget. THE REASON, and it is measurement not thrift: during the --ask trial a hard question (log entry 003) spent 0.074 of the 0.10 ceiling answering, and the next comparable question would have died mid-ReAct. A budget kill does not produce a cheaper answer, it produces a TRUNCATED one -- which during a trial whose whole purpose is comparing answer quality is noise injected into the data. WHAT THIS GIVES UP, recorded so nobody rediscovers it as a surprise: with budget_usd None, CostTracker.would_exceed() returns False always and the Stage-4.3.2 budget governor / downshift goes inert. A runaway ReAct loop is now bounded ONLY by max_iterations, not by spend. That is a real reduction in fail-closed protection and it was accepted deliberately. Pass --budget 0.50 to restore a ceiling for any single run; the flag still works and its help text now documents both the new default and what the default gives up. OBSERVED COSTS for calibration: trivial question 0.031 (7 calls), medium 0.055 (10 calls, continued session), hard 0.074 (11 calls). Verified after the change: live --ask reports budget_usd None / remaining_usd None and completes normally at 0.0335; Final Boss still 8/8. DIRECTIVE: if a future run ever produces a surprising bill, this entry is the cause -- re-impose a ceiling via --budget rather than assuming a pricing bug.

THE DIFFERENTIATING CAPABILITY WAS BUILT, WIRED, AND STARVED FOR 80 DAYS (found + fixed 2026-09-06). agent/life_state_monitor.py is the 'RAISE don't HOLD' channel -- proactive surfacing, fail-closed, never-nags, watermarked, registered as a SessionStart hook. A CLOSED LOOP in which the capability that would justify using the system is starved by not using the system. Meanwhile 535 turns of real work sat unconsolidated. WHY THIS IS THE SAME FAMILY AS KB 528: there, a usage log existed with no consumer. Here, a CAPABILITY existed with no instrument watching whether it still ran. In both cases the artifact was healthy-looking and dead, and nothing in the repo could represent its deadness. A system that cannot detect its own silent organs will keep building new ones. WHAT WAS ACTUALLY MISSING WAS TINY, and I nearly mis-scoped the fix as a re-plumb: CrossDomainCorrelationEngine ALREADY reads observation_queue.jsonl (correlation.py:86,357) -- the Claude Code capture stream. Deterministic template only (Rs0), once/day, fail-closed to exit 0, subprocess-timeout-bounded. Mind's heartbeat deliberately UNTOUCHED, so both sources feed one organ -- which was the user's explicit condition when choosing this option. ONE REAL BUG CAUGHT IN MY OWN FIX: I first rate-limited on the FEED having a today-entry. But when nothing clears the 0.60 floor no entry is written, so 'found nothing' would read as 'never ran' and the Stop hook would re-run the correlation engine on EVERY TURN. Corrected to rate-limit on ATTEMPT via behavioral_state_model.jsonl's mtime, which Consolidator persists on every run regardless of output. DIRECTIVE: unstarving is NOT the same as useful. THE FOUR GOALS COLLAPSE INTO ONE ORGAN (2026-09-06, canon re-scoped same day). After Codex concluded JARVIS is not the vehicle for 3 of the user's 4 goals, the user asked the right follow-up -- not 'is it over' but 'how COULD each goal be achievable via JARVIS'. Interrogating that produced a convergence. THE COUNTERFACTUAL TEST, which is the only honest way to ask this: what does JARVIS give the user that paying for a frontier subscription does not? Reasoning -- no. Context -- no. Knowledge -- no. Even personalization -- no, a frontier model matches it the moment you paste the right context. EXACTLY ONE THING SURVIVES: it cannot fire when you did not know to ask. Pasting requires knowing what you forgot. THE CAPABILITY IS THEREFORE 'unprompted surfacing over your own history', and all four goals reduce to it: work leverage = 'this reverses your July call, the reason then was Y'; frontier R&D = 'you tried this optical approach in March, it failed on brightness'; learning = 'you have been confused by this concept twice before'; ambient = NOT A GOAL, it is the DELIVERY CHANNEL for the other three. Four goals -> one organ + one channel, which is dramatically smaller than the twelve-specialist roster. TWO CONSEQUENCES, both written into the canon today. (1) The organ needs NO TRAINED ADAPTER -- it runs on the KB, consolidator and retrieval, all Stage 2/3 machinery already built. So ENDGAME Sec1.1 point 1's 'trained, not injected' is DEMOTED from settled deliverable to OPEN QUESTION in stage_5_specialists/ROADMAP.md, with the prior question stated explicitly: does a trained adapter beat the already-built retrieval+surfacing path on the user's real recurring work? Nobody has tested it, testing costs nothing, and it is a strict prerequisite to the Rs1,480-2,960 Engineer run because yes and no imply different quarters. (2) ENDGAME Sec3's twelve-specialist roster is flagged as architecture-if-justified, not a build plan -- ten of twelve have been deferred since 2026-08-10 and none has moved. (3) stage_6's 6.10 ambient is reframed as delivery channel with a hard ordering: ambient is worth exactly as much as the organ has to say, so build it only after the organ demonstrably produces insights worth interrupting someone for. DIRECTIVE: when asked what JARVIS is for, lead with unprompted surfacing, not with the roster, the adapter, or corpus depth. And do not cite roster completeness as a reason to build anything.

PROSE STATUS HEADERS ROT; STRUCTURED TABLES DO NOT (found and fixed 2026-09-03, surfaced BY an external audit). GENERALIZES KB 521, which found two files asserting a stale git status about themselves. This is the same failure at project scale, and the pattern is now sharp enough to state as a rule. THREE FILES CARRIED CONTRADICTORY 'where we are' CLAIMS: (1) .agent/rules/JARVIS_ENDGAME.md line 360 -- the document titled MASTER BLUEPRINT -- said 'Current Position: Stage 2, Sub-phase 2.5', four months and THREE STAGES stale, with its Sec7 table still marking Memory Layer as in-progress. (2) js-learning/JARVIS_MASTER_ROADMAP.md line 11 -- the file I had just told the user was authoritative -- said 'Stage 3 ... NOW: Sub-Phase 3.2', contradicting its OWN correct stage table twenty lines below it. (3) README.md was a single line, '# private-ai', for a 33K-line system. THE DISCRIMINATOR, and this is the reusable part: in every case the STRUCTURED TABLE was correct and the HUMAN-WRITTEN PARAGRAPH was stale. Tables get updated because a row maps to a task that visibly completes; a prose 'Current Position' sentence maps to nothing and has no owner, so no event ever fires to re-check it. USER ASKED (2026-09-02): 'if i have a bond then can the company fire me in that period?' -- i.e. whether the Celebal Service Commitment Period constrains the EMPLOYER as well as them. Answered against their real terms from KB 436 (Mutual Service Agreement signed 2026-04-16, SCP 24 months to 2027-04-22, flat 3-month notice running only AFTER the SCP, early-exit liability ~Rs 2,20,000 = Rs 1,50,000 + ~Rs 70,000 half-stipend). SUBSTANCE OF THE ANSWER: yes, they can terminate during the SCP -- a service bond is a one-way covenant binding the employee, and termination rights sit in a separate clause of the same document. BUT the more useful half is that if the EMPLOYER terminates without cause, they generally cannot then enforce the bond sum: the bond's consideration is the user's service, so a company that prevents performance cannot claim damages for the non-performance it caused, and Indian Contract Act s74 requires proof of ACTUAL loss with courts awarding reasonable compensation rather than the stipulated figure automatically (s27 voids restraint of trade, though service bonds tied to genuine training cost have been upheld since Niranjan Shankar Golikari v. Century Spinning, SC 1967). Practical note given more weight than the litigation angle: in Indian IT services the real leverage is almost never a lawsuit -- it is withholding the relieving letter and experience certificate, which the next employer asks for. WHY THEY ASKED IS UNKNOWN and I deliberately did not guess. Plausible readings, none confirmed: layoff or bench anxiety at Celebal; refining the 2027 exit plan; something specific happened at work; or abstract curiosity. FLAGGED FOR FOLLOW-UP -- if this recurs or sharpens, find out which, because the advice diverges: job-security worry needs the termination clause and notice-pay reading, exit planning needs the SCP math already in KB 436. ARCHITECTURE HIGHLIGHTS worth knowing before touching it: ONE job definition runs BOTH legs, selected by an env=src|tgt parameter, with four control-plane condition_task gates so the off-leg tasks are SKIPPED rather than started-and-exited (the gates exist for COST -- without them the tgt leg provisions an 8-16 node E32 cluster twice to run two notebooks that immediately exit). The src leg triggers the opposite REGION's copy of itself over the Jobs REST API with an Entra SP, fires-and-exits, and waits in a separate task. Joins use run_if AT_LEAST_ONE_SUCCESS specifically because exactly one of two inbound edges is live per leg -- ALL_SUCCESS would be permanently unreachable and ALL_DONE would let a genuine trigger failure through. The framework SPLITS CHECKS ACROSS TWO CLUSTER TYPES by which store answers them: UC/serverless for catalog reads, and data_security_mode NONE with direct SP OAuth for anything needing VERSION AS OF on a row-filtered/column-masked table (UC's session analyzer blocks both path-reads and time-travel on those, and there is no config that keeps UC on and skips the check). Size-tiering (l/s) routes work to differently-shaped clusters, with the tier decided in the MERGE step because a population statistic cannot be computed inside a for_each fan-out. Three terminal branches, nothing joins them back. VERDICT MODEL: three verdicts not two -- PASS / FAIL / NOT MEASURED, where NOT MEASURED is never folded into FAIL, because 'we were not allowed to look' and 'the clone lost the data' are opposite conclusions. CORRECTION to Data_Engineering_Lessons.md line 489 (found 2026-08-22 on reading the actual framework code). My 2026-08-08 lesson 'Time Travel Is Bounded by Retention' states Delta's window as 7 days / 168h and prescribes gating every resolved historical version on 'now() - commit_ts > 168h'. That is the framework's SUPERSEDED behaviour, and tst_tables_version_retention_check.py now documents at length why it was wrong. THE REAL MECHANISM IS TWO INDEPENDENT CLOCKS: deletedFileRetentionDuration (default 7d) governs how long VACUUM keeps tombstoned DATA FILES; logRetentionDuration (default 30d) governs how long _delta_log commits/checkpoints survive.
